papers.trackName: Retinal AI and Computational Ophthalmology
papers.title: LightHybridNet: A Lightweight Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Efficient Multi-Label Ophthalmic Disease Classification in Imbalanced Fundus Images
authors: Hem Raj Dadral Najam Ul Hasan
papers.summary: Eye diseases are a major global cause of blindness and vision impairment, highlighting the need for accurate and early diagnosis to prevent further deterioration. Despite advances in medical imaging, classifying retinal diseases from fundus images remains challenging due to the complexity and subtlety of visual features. This study aims to develop and validate LightHybridNet, a novel lightweight hybrid deep learning framework, to improve the classification of eye diseases from fundus images. The model incorporates architectural features, such as depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling mechanisms, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and robustness. To validate the model, the ODIR-5K dataset, comprising 8 disease categories, was used. To enhance image quality, pre-processing approaches were applied, including histogram equalisation, colour space conversion, and contrast adjustment, resulting in high-resolution images. Furthermore, image augmentation was employed to increase the dataset size, thereby improving the model's ability to generalise during training. The hybrid architecture helps the model concentrate on relevant image regions while capturing and integrating details at different scales, significantly improving classification performance. To evaluate its effectiveness, the model was compared with transfer-learning models. The results show that LightHybridNet outperforms the baselines, achieving a weighted F1-score of 91.51%, a macro AUC of 98.26%, and a Cohen's Kappa of 90.14% on the validation set. Furthermore, model interpretability was enhanced using explainable AI methods, including Grad-CAM, to identify and emphasise features influencing the decision-making process. LightHybridNet represents a promising advancement in automated ocular disease detection, offering improved diagnostic reliability for clinical use.

papers.trackName: Post-Quantum Cryptography and Embedded Systems Security
papers.title: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking
papers.summary:
Neural watermarking systems are typically trained as tightly coupled embedder-detector pairs and implicitly assume static deployment. In real-world deployments, embedders and detectors are frequently updated and selectively decoupled for security and versioning purposes, which can break detection in previously embedded content and, more critically, increase false-positive rates on embedders that a given detector is intentionally not intended to recognize.
  In this paper the concept of backward compatibility in zero-bit audio watermarking is formalized. A training framework is proposed that pairs a new detector with a sequence of frozen legacy embedders (its legacy chain), using a performance-weighted sampling strategy so that the detector retains accuracy across all earlier versions. This coupling, while necessary for backward compatibility, is shown to induce an embedder-collapse effect that catastrophically degrades the true negative rate (TNR) against out-of-chain embedders. To counteract this, a Angular Diversity Loss (ADL) is introduced that explicitly forces each new embedder to occupy a distinct region of the output space. The combined approach restores near-perfect TNR with no measurable cost to detection accuracy or perceptual audio quality.

papers.trackName: AI-Driven Cybersecurity and Secure Healthcare Systems
papers.title: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
papers.summary: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a private benchmark of 120 held-out repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 73 CWE types, eight languages, and all OWASP Top 10 2025 categories. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a programmatic verifier. We validated the verifier against a panel of agentic judges, manually reviewing disagreements during development and refining the checks. The best agents reach 68% pass@1 and 81% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with the same pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or vulnerability categories, and difficulty varies far more by vulnerability category than by language. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.

papers.trackName: Trustworthy and Privacy-Preserving AI
papers.title: Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network for Interpretable Big Data Analytics and Secure Cloud Decision-Making Systems
papers.summary: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. This paper presents the Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network, a deep learning framework that integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) mechanisms. The architecture combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) for temporal feature extraction, Transformer encoders for contextual modeling, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for inter-feature dependency analysis. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates these representations. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and an explanation loss are incorporated to improve interpretability and explanation consistency. The framework is designed for deployment in a federated cloud architecture, using homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based auditing to support data privacy and accountability. Experimental evaluations across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets report 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, and a 98.0% F1-score, outperforming the evaluated CNN-LSTM, Transformer-only, and XGBoost baselines. Under projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial perturbations, the model reportedly retains accuracy above 91.5%. Scalability experiments report throughput of 80,000 messages per second with latency below 200 milliseconds. These results suggest that the proposed framework has potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems.

papers.trackName: Medical Imaging and Multimodal Biomedical AI
papers.title: Continual pretraining Prostate MRI ViT Encoder for task alignment
papers.summary: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. Unlike language models, where the two stages are naturally aligned, such alignment is less evident in vision based applications. Motivated by this gap, we explore continual pretraining. Specifically, continually pretraining a pretrained ViT encoder using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a prostate segmentation task to enhance task alignment and downstream performance. We further perform layer-wise representational analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to assess representational shifts and their correlation with task outcomes. Our experiments show improved performance in 3 of 6 downstream tasks and comparable results in the others. Our Feature analysis reveals that, for segmentation tasks, continually pretrained encoder features exhibit greater similarity to those of the finetuned encoder than the original pretrained encoder, correlating with observed performance gains.

papers.trackName: Retinal AI and Computational Ophthalmology
papers.title: International Multi-Centre Validation of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Precise Discrimination between Normal and Abnormal Retinal Development
papers.summary: Arrested retinal development can cause childhood visual impairment, but grading optical coherence tomography scans is difficult to standardise across devices and centres. We developed and evaluated an unsupervised domain adaptation model to classify normal and abnormal retinal development across different OCT systems. This retrospective multicentre study used OCT scans from five centres in four countries and the UK Biobank. Data covered four OCT devices, including table mounted and handheld systems. A ResNet50 based Domain Adversarial Neural Network was trained using labelled images from a source device and unlabelled images from a target device. We evaluated six source to target pairings and compared model performance with seven clinician graders. A separate Heidelberg Spectralis dataset was reserved for external evaluation. Across validation sets, accuracy ranged from 87.75% to 96.06%, sensitivity from 88.68% to 98.38%, and specificity from 78.00% to 98.02%. The best performing model, adapted from TM OCT1 to HH OCT1, achieved 96.06% accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.994, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.981 to 0.999. Several models also maintained discrimination on the unseen Heidelberg device. Unsupervised domain adaptation enabled OCT classification across devices without labelled target device data. The approach may support more consistent assessment of retinal development and large scale analysis of existing imaging datasets.

papers.trackName: Post-Quantum Cryptography and Embedded Systems Security
papers.title: Combining Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution: Taxonomy, Constructions, Proofs, Standards, Deployments and Open Problems
papers.summary: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) address the quantum threat from opposite directions: PQC replaces vulnerable public-key algorithms with schemes believed to resist quantum cryptanalysis, while QKD derives keys whose secrecy rests on physical assumptions rather than computational ones. Because each approach has a distinct failure mode, a growing body of work combines them so that a session key remains secure if either component holds. We first establish the deployed baseline, hybrid classical-plus-PQC key exchange, against which QKD-augmented designs must be judged. We then propose a taxonomy of hybrid PQC-QKD designs along eight dimensions (integration layer, combiner construction, authentication scope and source, QKD topology, trusted entities, key-delivery interface, classical component, and evidence type), and use it to compare published protocols, including Muckle and its successors, MACsec and TLS integrations, and IKEv2 mechanisms standardised in RFCs 8784, 9370, and 9867. We examine key-combiner constructions in light of the KEM-combiner literature and of NIST, ETSI, and ITU-T guidance, and map the security arguments for hybrid PQC-QKD protocols onto a common grid of security model, assumptions, permitted compromise, established guarantee, and limitations. We synthesise deployment evidence from metropolitan and national QKD networks, distinguishing the few testbeds that have run PQC in the key path from pure-QKD deployments, and summarise the standards and policy landscape, including the positions of national security agencies that recommend against relying on QKD alone. We close with open problems: authentication of the QKD classical channel, shared-infrastructure threat models, device certification versus formal proofs, formal verification of hybrid handshakes, and the lack of peer-reviewed deployment economics.

papers.trackName: AI-Driven Cybersecurity and Secure Healthcare Systems
papers.title: Mind the gap: a mixed-methods analysis of the cybersecurity knowledge–behavior discrepancy in public Wi-Fi usage
papers.venue: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
papers.summary:
Purpose 
                     This paper aims to examine whether perceived public Wi-Fi risk and declarative familiarity with wireless-network security concepts translate into consistent protective behavior. It focuses on the cybersecurity knowledge–behavior discrepancy in public Wi-Fi usage and contextualizes this discrepancy alongside exposure to rogue access points (RAPs). 
                   
                   
                     Design/methodology/approach 
                     The study applies an exploratory mixed-methods design consisting of two analytically separate components: a cross-sectional survey of primarily working-age respondents (n = 177) and a zero-payload observational field experiment. The survey examined perceived public Wi-Fi risk, wireless-security familiarity, virtual private network (VPN) usage, service set identifier (SSID) verification and auto-connect configuration. The field component deployed non-capturing RAPs in public locations to observe aggregate Layer-2 device-association events without linking observed devices to survey respondents or collecting credentials, payload content, direct personal identifiers or application-layer traffic. 
                   
                   
                     Findings 
                     Although 71.2% of respondents identified unsecured public Wi-Fi as a cybersecurity risk, many risk-aware respondents still reported inconsistent protective behavior, including irregular VPN usage and infrequent SSID verification. Non-parametric analyses indicated significant behavioral differences across threat-perception categories, but stronger threat perception did not eliminate risky operational behavior. The field component recorded 27 device-association events, including both user-initiated and automated association events. These observations are interpreted as contextual evidence of exposure mechanisms, not as prevalence estimates or population-level susceptibility rates. 
                   
                   
                     Practical implications 
                     The paper contributes to behavioral information security by distinguishing between user-level mitigation inconsistency and device-level structural exposure in public Wi-Fi environments. 
                   
                   
                     Originality/value 
                     The paper contributes to behavioral information security by contextualizing the cybersecurity knowledge–behavior discrepancy in public Wi-Fi environments. It juxtaposes survey-based evidence of self-reported awareness and mitigation behavior with contextual observational evidence of RAP associations, while explicitly distinguishing between user-level mitigation inconsistency and device-level structural exposure.

papers.trackName: Trustworthy and Privacy-Preserving AI
papers.title: Federated Art Chase: Privacy Leakage and Data Poisoning in Federated Fine-Tuning
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used to adapt a pretrained, centrally fine-tuned model to data that remain on user devices, beyond training a model from scratch. In this report, prepared for the 4th Federated Machine Learning International Summer School, we study the privacy and integrity of this approach with a reproducible pipeline. An ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV4-Conv-Small model is fine-tuned centrally on ten Quick, Draw! classes (97.50% test accuracy) and then adapted with head-only FedAvg over ten non-IID clients, which raises client training accuracy from 90.34% to 91.49% while preserving global accuracy. We evaluate four adversarial scenarios. First, from a single one-step client update, an honest-but-curious server recovers the complete private label set, but its reconstructions follow class prototypes rather than the private drawings (mean SSIM 0.130). Second, from a one-round FedAvg aggregate, label-count recovery falls from 87.5% with one client to 75.0% with five and ten clients, below the 80.0% of an uninformed uniform guess. Third, under FedAvg, a backdoor injected by 30%, 50%, and 100% of the clients reaches an attack success rate (ASR) of 21.9%, 31.3%, and 54.7% at a cost of at most 0.8 percentage points of clean accuracy, whereas label flipping is effective only when most of the source-class data are relabeled. Fourth, FLTrust with a root set retained from centralized fine-tuning lowers the backdoor ASR to 1.8% and 4.0% at 30% and 50% malicious clients and the label-flipping ASR from 12.6% to 0.8% without measurable clean-accuracy loss, but provides no protection when every client is malicious. The report closes with a live session in which participants draw, fine-tune, and poison the model through Indigma's FedMaestro orchestrator. Code and executed notebooks, runnable on Google Colab, are at https://github.com/Indigma-Innovations/fl-summer-school.

papers.trackName: Medical Imaging and Multimodal Biomedical AI
papers.title: MedPAO-VL: Interpretable and Protocol-Compliant Agent for Structured Radiology Report Generation
papers.summary: Despite the remarkable generalization capabilities of Large Language Models, generating clinically accurate and structured radiology reports from medical images remains a significant challenge. Current end-to-end approaches function as black boxes, prone to factual hallucinations and generating ungrounded findings. This lack of reliability and failure to adhere to domain-specific structuring protocols, fundamentally limits their clinical utility. We present MedPAO-VL, a multimodal agent that shifts the paradigm from monolithic generation to explainable, iterative, protocol-compliant structured report generation. Unlike deterministic models, our plan-act-observe loop functions as a goal-oriented agent: it first perceives the Chest X-Ray through an explainable vision module designed to capture inherent diagnostic uncertainty, then iteratively refines the generated report by observing semantic discrepancies and self-correcting its generation for better alignment with visually detected clinical findings. Evaluation of our framework demonstrates that this agentic reasoning improves clinical correctness and completeness, achieving an expert-rated accuracy score of 3.5/5 and a structural score of 4.3/5. By prioritizing pathology specific explainability and iterative refinement over opaque end-to-end mapping, MedPAO-VL offers a transparent and clinically viable alternative for automated structured radiology report generation.

papers.title: Performance Characterization of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
papers.summary: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. Under conservative signal conditions, Pulsar's Combinatorial Watermark, where 21 ranging code chips are inverted among the 1023, provides 32-bit authentication security each second. In this work, we present our software-defined radio (SDR) implementation of the Pulsar watermark processor. We discuss various threat models, multiple receiver architectures, implications to the receiver, and results from using Pulsar's SDR processing watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission. Our results demonstrate the feasible implementation of Pulsar's watermark verification process in commercial GNSS receivers. This is an important milestone in making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers later this year after deployment of our first four production satellites.

papers.title: Facial Expression and Behavior Modeling from Digital Avatars to Expressive Humanoid Robots: A Review
papers.summary:
Endowing humanoid robots with expressive, controllable, and robust facial expressions and behaviors is essential for advancing human-like humanoid-human interaction across social, healthcare, and service domains. papers.title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
papers.summary: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. papers.title: Quantum-Resilient Secure Protocol for Decentralized Edge-IoT Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading Systems
papers.summary: The rise of quantum computing presents substantial challenges to the security of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) energy trading systems. This paper introduces an innovative mutual authenticated session key agreement protocol aimed at protecting edge-IoT P2P energy trading communications in the quantum era. Each peer is an IoT-enabled smart metering device that is registered by an edge registration authority and acts as both producer and consumer. The proposed protocol incorporates CRYSTALS-Kyber's quantum-resistant cryptographic suite to guarantee the authenticity and confidentiality of negotiated session keys in the presence of quantum threats. Furthermore, it leverages the Hedera Hashgraph public blockchain, which is recognized for its quantum-resilient design, to ensure transparency and support efficient revocation mechanisms. Extensive comparative analyses have been conducted to demonstrate the protocol's superiority over existing alternatives, including both traditional schemes based on classical cryptography and emerging early-stage post-quantum approaches, in terms of performance and security features. By combining robust security and high efficiency, the proposed protocol fosters the development of resilient decentralized energy markets, paving the way for secure and sustainable energy distribution in the future.

papers.title: Securing artificial intelligence in human resource management: a systematic review and the AI-HRM cybersecurity architecture (AHCA)
papers.venue: ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS)
papers.summary:
Purpose 
                     This study aims to address the information security governance issues associated with the use of AI in HRM by developing the artificial intelligence–human resource management (AI-HRM) cybersecurity architecture (AHCA), a novel domain-specific architecture. 
                   
                   
                     Design/methodology/approach 
                     The review followed the PRISMA 2020 principles, and 72 peer-reviewed papers were obtained from journals indexed in Scopus and IEEE Xplore, or from CORE-ranked journals, for the years 2020–2025, with citation chaining in Google Scholar. Three research questions guided the synthesis, covering threat conceptualisation, security implications and governance. This study then created the AHCA following an iterative design science process, using each component directly from literature reviews, and constructed a structured rubric with explicit anchoring examples to enable replication of the comparative evaluation. 
                   
                   
                     Findings 
                     The review identified six categories of AI-HRM security threats: data breaches (T1), exploitation of algorithmic bias (T2), insider threat amplification (T3), model poisoning attacks (T4), regulatory non-compliance (T5) and governance and audit failures (T6). There is a wide disparity in the attention these subjects receive in the literature: algorithmic bias (43.1 %) and governance and audit failure (51.4 %) together account for 94.4 % of the corpus whose primary focus could be coded, while data breaches (1.4 %), insider threat (1.4 %) and regulatory non-compliance (2.8 %) sit at the margins, and no study takes model poisoning as its primary focus. In addition, most governance-oriented research identifies accountability gaps but stops short of architectural solutions. The AHCA is designed to address this structural deficit, pairing four-layer architecture with a 14-indicator security performance indicator (SPI) framework. 
                   
                   
                     Research limitations/implications 
                     The corpus is limited to English-language publications from 2020 to 2025 that appear in journals in the AHCA’s Q1 or Q2 tiers, and the AHCA itself is a design artefact that will be tested in practice through Delphi panels of experts and longitudinal case studies. The technical security literature emerged when searching IEEE Xplore and Scopus; a complementary search of the ACM Digital Library is planned as a future extension. 
                   
                   
                     Practical implications 
                     The AHCA and its SPI framework offer HR practitioners and policymakers an AI-HRM-specific blueprint for general data protection regulation (GDPR) compliant, high-risk employment systems in accordance with the provisions of the European Union AI Act. 
                   
                   
                     Originality/value 
                     The AHCA incorporates GDPR and EU AI Act compliance-by-design principles into a single HRM-specific security architecture that is currently in the early phases of development. It is the only benchmark that addresses the HRM-specific and EU AI Act dimensions, which are not addressed by sector-agnostic comparators, and it performs well in the generic HRM security dimensions on a replicable nine-dimension rubric, benchmarked against NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, ISO 27001 and NIST CSF.

papers.title: Byzantine-Resilient Federated Large Language Model via Hypergraph Message Passing
papers.summary: Federated Large Language Models (FedLLMs) are promising to deliver privacy-preserving, collaborative intelligence. The decentralized training process is vulnerable to Byzantine attacks that corrupt semantic consistency and factual resilience through malicious model updates. This paper presents a new resilience strategy that prevents semantically corrupted knowledge from propagating during federated aggregation. A defense problem is formulated to jointly maximize global accuracy and suppress manipulated model updates, enabling trustworthy knowledge aggregation without accessing private local data. To strengthen the resilience of FedLLMs, we develop a novel Hypergraph Message Passing Graph Autoencoder (HMP-GAE) framework, where low-rank model updates are represented as nodes in a hypergraph and high-order semantic relationships among multiple agents are exploited through iterative message passing. By leveraging historical checkpoints and cross-agent relational reasoning, HMP-GAE identifies and suppresses semantically inconsistent updates while preserving knowledge alignment among agents throughout federated training. HMP-GAE is implemented using Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.2 as pretrained FedLLM backbones and evaluated on AG News and Yahoo! Answers datasets. Compared to existing defenses, HMP-GAE improves global accuracy by $1.21$\%, reduces final-model classification semantic entropy by $44.08$\%, and lowers perplexity by $13.34$\%. HMP-GAE outperforms the GAE-based defense by improving the accuracy $1.39$\%, reducing the semantic entropy by $54.5$\%, and lowering perplexity by $35.5$\%.

papers.trackName: Medical Imaging and Multimodal Biomedical AI
papers.title: MID: Mask-Image Distributional Divergence for Evaluating Medical Image Segmentation
papers.summary: Current evaluation protocols for medical image segmentation remain largely anchored in sample-wise comparisons, e.g., Dice and Hausdorff distance, which require each prediction to be paired with a ground-truth mask. Yet two limitations arise in practice: they are inapplicable when predictions are made on unlabeled data; and even when annotations are available, they cannot assess whether a collection of predictions matches the distributional structure of the ground-truth population. We introduce MID (Mask-Image Distributional Divergence), a distribution-level evaluation metric for medical image segmentation. MID builds upon the observation that segmentation quality is a property of the joint image-mask distribution: a mask may be anatomically plausible in isolation yet incorrect for the image it accompanies. MID compares the joint distribution of images and masks between a reference set and a set of predictions, without requiring sample-wise correspondence. This captures both mask realism and image-mask consistency. We evaluate MID across 13 publicly available datasets spanning CT, MRI, and MRA. Under anatomically realistic corruptions across 56 organ groups, MID tracks mean Dice and Hausdorff distance without per-sample ground-truth pairing. MID also detects distributional shifts across modalities and anatomies, identifies image-mask misalignment through controlled shuffling experiments, and produces reliable model rankings across real segmentation models. Official implementation available at github.com/erc-caravel/pytorch-mid

papers.title: Towards Efficient Threat Intelligence Instruction Tuning via Quality-Aware and Optimal Transport-Guided Data Selection
papers.summary: High-quality data is essential for improving instruction tuning in threat intelligence analysis. However, existing methods for generating cybersecurity instruction data lack reliable quality assessment mechanisms, and gradient influence-based data selection methods primarily focus on single-sample matching, failing to cover diverse and complex security capabilities. To address these issues, we propose CTI-TDS, a Targeted Data Selection method for instruction tuning in Cyber Threat Intelligence analysis. Specifically, we first filter high-quality CTI instructions by integrating instruction style consistency and security knowledge verification. Furthermore, we formulate gradient influence as a distribution alignment problem, learning a gradient subspace of target tasks and applying entropic regularized optimal transport to optimize distribution matching between training samples and target tasks, enabling diversity-aware data selection. We conduct extensive experiments on CTIBench across multiple large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that when fine-tuning with only a small set of high-value instruction data, CTI-TDS outperforms existing data selection methods and achieves competitive performance on threat intelligence analysis tasks.

papers.title: Federated Distillation: A Survey
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing clients’ raw data, but parameter exchange can impose substantial communication costs and usually requires compatible model architectures. Federated distillation (FD) instead transfers predictive or intermediate knowledge through knowledge distillation (KD), which can support heterogeneous models and reduce communication in suitable settings. These benefits are not automatic: their magnitude depends on the transmitted knowledge, reference data, communication schedule, and threat model. This survey provides a challenge-centered synthesis of FD. We first formalize a representative public-data, response-based FD protocol and then organize existing methods by the FL challenges they address, including data, system, and model heterogeneity, client drift, catastrophic forgetting, communication cost, and privacy risk. We further review applications in industrial engineering, computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare, including recent federated adaptation of large language models. Finally, we identify five research priorities: richer transferred knowledge, joint treatment of interacting forms of heterogeneity, communication-aware distillation, threat-model-driven privacy protection, and standardized theory, benchmarks, and evaluation.

papers.title: Exploring the Latent Structure of AMD Severity Using Retinal Foundation Models
papers.summary: Retinal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, yet relatively little is known about how disease-related information is represented within their learned embeddings and whether this distribution influences downstream prediction performance. In this work, we use Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) as a case study to investigate how disease severity is represented within the embedding space of RET-CLIP, a retinal vision-language foundation model, using bilateral fundus images from the AREDS dataset, benchmarked against non-retinal encoders. We first characterize the distribution of AMD severity within the learned representation space and then evaluate how this structure influences classification performance across three clinically relevant task formulations of increasing granularity. Finally, we analyze the most influential latent dimensions combining feature attribution, statistical phenotype association, and qualitative image analyses. Our results show that RET-CLIP represents AMD severity as a continuous spectrum rather than a set of discrete categories, with healthy and advanced disease stages exhibiting clearer separation than intermediate ones. This organization was reflected in downstream performance, which decreased from a balanced accuracy of 0.844 and 0.814 for binary AMD and Late-AMD detection respectively to 0.446 for six-class grading. Furthermore, the most influential latent dimensions were statistically associated to distinct retinal phenotypes, including drusen accumulation, pigmentary alterations, and advanced retinal lesions. These findings suggest that the structure of retinal foundation-model representations influences the difficulty of clinically relevant prediction tasks and demonstrate the potential of representation-level analysis for understanding disease organization and improving interpretability.

papers.title: Closed-loop evaluation of LLM agents for embedded software development
papers.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as coding agents that edit files, run builds and tests, inspect execution results, and repair software iteratively. Embedded firmware is a demanding target because correctness depends on closed-loop behavior under sensing, timing, and safety constraints, not only on static source quality. Yet embedded-agent evaluation remains limited and often emphasizes one-shot synthesis or offline correctness.
  We present a benchmark for closed-loop evaluation of embedded coding agents. Each task provides a plain-text engineering description, constrained workspace, and visible build-and-runtime surface. The agent must translate requirements into implementation and self-verification steps, then iterate until the required device behavior is achieved. The suite contains five embedded-control tasks and four feedback scenarios: one-shot generation, realistic self-verification, CI-style red/green feedback, and oracle-style detailed feedback.
  The implementation targets simulated ESP32 firmware for reproducibility. We evaluate seven GPT-family and Qwen-family configurations across five tasks and four scenarios, with three repetitions per condition for 420 runs. gpt-5.4 has the highest pass rate among evaluated configurations but does not saturate the benchmark; qwen3.5-27B is the strongest observed local model; and smaller local models degrade sharply in pass rate and search efficiency. These results suggest that capable local embedded coding agents are emerging.

papers.title: Tanchun: Robust Flow-Based HTTP(S) DDoS Detection via Behavioral Attribute Guidance
papers.summary:
HTTP(S) DDoS attacks have surged in frequency and scale, posing a significant threat to network security. Flow-based detection is a promising solution for large-scale HTTP(S) DDoS detection due to its decryption-free operation and scalability. However, the coarse-grained numerical statistics in flow data limit accurate attack detection and lack robustness when benign and attack traffic patterns drift over time.
  In this paper, we present Tanchun, a drift-aware flow-based HTTP(S) DDoS detection system that relies solely on decryption-free flow data. Specifically, Tanchun groups flows by IP-pair and aggregates them over consecutive time slots into behavior sequences, capturing temporal access patterns to compensate for the limited information in individual flows. It further abstracts these sequences into human-understandable behavioral attributes that capture stable behavioral semantics. Tanchun then aligns behavior sequences with their corresponding behavioral attributes to guide representation learning, enabling robust detection under traffic drift.
  We evaluate Tanchun across diverse HTTP(S) DDoS scenarios. Tanchun achieves the best overall performance, with an average F1-score of 0.988, and outperforms the second-best method by 5.3\% and 9.6\% under benign-traffic and attack-traffic drift, respectively. Experiments on real-world traffic traces further demonstrate its practical effectiveness.

papers.title: ReGraph: A Computational Account of Emergent Generalization in the "what" and "where" Dual Visual Streams
papers.summary: Where generalization capacity--the ability to extract context-invariant relational structures--first emerges remains a central question in AI and neuroscience. The foundation for this capacity lies upstream of the hippocampus, within the entorhinal cortex, where parallel pathways dissociate relational structure in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) from sensory content in the lateral entorhinal cortex. However, as Eichenbaum argued, such factorization likely originates earlier, driven by the segregation of the dorsal ('where') and ventral ('what') visual streams. Supporting this, grid-like firing patterns--a signature of MEC (context-invariant codes)--also appear in preceding neocortical regions along the dorsal pathway. Yet, how such representations are computationally formed along upstream pathways remains unknown. To investigate this in silico, we developed ReGraph, a recurrent dual-stream graph model with biological inductive biases, including retina-driven stream-specialized encoding, dorsal-to-ventral modulation, and dynamic lateral connectivity. Trained on the action benchmark Something-Something V2, ReGraph revealed a pathway-specific emergence of relational mapping: context-invariant codes and grid-like spatial bases uniquely co-emerged along the extended dorsal stream. In contrast, their absence in single-stream, unmodulated variants, and standard baselines implies that these inductive biases are prerequisites for relational structures. Crucially, our post-hoc analyses demonstrated that these grid-like bases serve as reusable routing templates for information processing via lateral connectivity. Together, our findings provide a computational account that generalization may not be a faculty that emerges abruptly within a dedicated region, but a property that already takes shape as sensory information is parsed into factorized streams of hierarchical visual processing.

papers.title: Provable Subexponential Algorithms for NIST Third-Round Lattice Families
papers.summary:
We give provable classical subexponential algorithms for secret recovery in growing parameter families associated with NIST third-round lattice candidates. For the Kyber/ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, SABER, NTRU LPRime, and Dilithium/ML-DSA families studied here, polynomial moduli and polylogarithmic coefficient scales yield recovery of the short secret component in expected time and space $2^{(1/2+o(1))n/\ln\ln n}$.
  For noisy or rounded linear relations, we exploit an exact gap in the squared Euclidean norm of a comparison vector defined by each coordinate guess. One Gaussian list suffices to identify every secret coordinate by binary search, without enumerating the others. We establish the required sampling guarantees through new geometric bounds for structured public operators over prime and power of two moduli. The construction builds on the Wagner-style Gaussian sampling framework of Ducas, Engelberts, and Loyer (CRYPTO 2025) and the low-error decision-LWE algorithm of Han, Gao, and Hu (2026).
  For quotient relations of NTRU type, we develop an affine slice search: fixing coordinates restricts candidate pairs to slices of the public lattice, and their estimated Gaussian masses guide the choice of each next coordinate. In the stated modulus window, Falcon's key generation quality condition supplies the required mass bound. The algorithm then recovers an equivalent signing key with high probability in time and space $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$. The same search recovers the short key core for cyclic NTRU-HPS/HRSS.
  Together, these results give subexponential algorithms for problem families associated with all seven NIST third-round lattice candidates. Despite the subexponential complexity, our results do not establish a reduction in the concrete security of the currently specified parameter sets.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Cyber-Physical Risk-Aware Power Grid Operations
papers.summary: Power grid cyber-physical security requires intrusion detection methods that account for the operational consequences of detection errors. However, the existing intrusion detection approaches primarily focus on the predictive performance of learning algorithms, while downstream operational costs are often optimized independently, which can lead to inferior operational performance. papers.title: Private and Distributionally Robust Federated Multiclass Classification
papers.summary: Fault diagnosis in asset-intensive industries requires multiclass models trained on noisy, sensitive data collected across geographically distributed client sites. Federated learning enables collaborative training without centralizing data, but most approaches do not provide formal privacy guarantees for individual records stored at client sites and can degrade under label noise. We build on a federated Wasserstein distributionally robust multiclass objective with the Crammer-Singer loss, solved using an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based algorithm. To protect the released client updates, our method injects calibrated Gaussian noise into the proximal linearized client updates of both the local model and the local distributionally robust variable before aggregation at the central server, and we quantify the cumulative privacy loss using the moments accountant. We provide per-round sample-level $(ε,δ)$-differential privacy guarantees and an overall composed privacy guarantee across all training rounds, together with convergence results and an explicit privacy-utility tradeoff. Experiments on simulated industrial fault data and UCI benchmark datasets show that our method outperforms differentially private federated empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent baselines in most tested settings, with the largest gains under strong privacy-induced noise.

papers.title: Quantifying Volumetric Risk: Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction for 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.summary: Reliable volumetric segmentation is critical for clinical diagnostics, yet foundation models such as MedSAM remain deterministic and lack calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift. On both benchmarks the 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval for the observed coverage of CA-WCP contains the nominal 90\% level for every semantic class, while interval width is reduced by 8--14\% relative to symmetric weighted conformal prediction. We further encode the calibrated intervals into structured prompts for a multimodal large language model to produce uncertainty-conditioned radiology reports, linking distribution-shift-aware uncertainty quantification to interpretable clinical communication.

papers.summary: Clinical diagnosis is inherently a structured reasoning process, yet existing deep learning models often bypass this structure by mapping image features directly to disease labels without explicitly interrogating the morphological and textural criteria that clinicians systematically evaluate. This limits diagnostic transparency and may compromise safe clinical deployment. For each input image, MedCORE decomposes the diagnostic process into clinically defined criteria, spatially localizes each criterion to diagnostically relevant image regions, encodes evidence through multi-scale representations that capture macro-structural and micro-textural pathological characteristics, and refines criterion representations using a Graph Attention Network that explicitly models inter-criteria dependencies. Criterion representations are further aligned with clinical text descriptors, reinforced through class-wise visual prototypes, and aggregated using uncertainty-calibrated weighting that proportionally discounts low-confidence diagnostic evidence. MedCORE is validated across three clinically heterogeneous imaging modalities, including dermoscopic lesion classification on ISIC 2018, breast ultrasound lesion characterization on BUSI, and diabetic retinopathy grading on IDRiD. These results demonstrate consistent improvements over strong CNN, transformer, biomedical vision-language, concept-based, and prototype-based baselines.

papers.title: A Zero-Knowledge Signature Framework for Efficient Post-Quantum Message Authentication in Cooperative Automated Driving
papers.summary: Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAV) rely on authenticated Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications to exchange safety-critical information among vehicles and roadside infrastructure. As the automotive industry transitions toward post-quantum cryptography (PQC), the significantly larger public keys and signatures of standardized PQC digital signature algorithms introduce substantial communication overhead, which challenges the scalability of certificate-based V2X authentication, particularly for high-frequency cooperative awareness messages (CAM). This paper presents ZKS-PQC, a zero-knowledge signature framework that enables communication-efficient post-quantum message authentication for cooperative V2X systems. Instead of transmitting complete post-quantum public keys and signatures, the proposed framework replaces this authentication material with a compact Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) while preserving compatibility with existing certificate-based trust architectures. This approach supports incremental migration and backward compatibility with the legacy ECDSA. The framework is implemented using the Open Quantum Safe (liboqs) and ZKP (Bulletproofs) libraries, and we evaluated the performance of standardized NIST PQC signature algorithms and additional candidate algorithms. Experimental validation on both a Linux platform and a commercial On-Board Unit (OBU) demonstrates substantial reductions in message size exceeding 95% for all algorithms, while limiting additional processing overhead by staying within the order of milliseconds at both sender and receiver in many algorithms, consistent with the latency requirements of real-time V2X operation. By decoupling communication overhead from the size characteristics of post-quantum signature algorithms, ZKS-PQC offers a practical migration strategy for scalable, quantum-resilient message authentication in future CAV systems.

papers.title: Quantization-Tolerant Gradient Auditing for Active Inference-Attack Detection in Federated Learning
papers.summary: Inside a federated learning system a participant can quietly study the shared model and learn about others' private data. The usual defense, differential privacy, often adds so much noise that the model is no longer worth training. An attacker that answers the challenge on an untouched copy of the model while tampering with a replica evades the audit entirely. Therefore the checksum is a reliable in-band signal against attackers that do not decouple the audited computation from the attacked one, and it composes with differential privacy, whose accuracy cost we quantify on Texas100, rather than replacing it.

papers.title: A4-MR: Abnormality-aware Anatomical Alignment for MR
papers.summary: Recent advances in large-scale foundation models have enabled strong generalization across a wide range of clinical and research tasks in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, existing vision-language MRI models remain limited in anatomy-specific localization and pathology-aware representation, particularly in real-world settings. We introduce A4-MR, a 3D vision-language foundation model trained on approximately 50,000 MRI studies comprising 491,000 series, roughly half of which are paired with radiology reports. A4-MR is designed to: (1) learn anatomy localization through large-scale pretraining with noisy labels; (2) align image and text representations at the anatomical level; and (3) learn distinct representations of healthy and abnormal anatomy. Across a diverse set of downstream tasks, A4-MR outperforms existing foundation models, including a +1.7 AUROC improvement over MedSigLIP for abnormality detection. Using a frozen encoder, A4-MR also surpasses an end-to-end task-specific MedNeXt model for knee segmentation by +1.4 Dice and performs comparably to the best task-specific model for abdominal organ segmentation on AMOS, within 0.4 Dice. Finally, without anatomical prompts, A4-MR localizes 3D anatomy comparably to MedSAM2 provided with ground-truth bounding boxes. Together, these results demonstrate that anatomy-level multimodal alignment and abnormality-aware representation learning can enable a single MRI foundation model to support localization, segmentation, and pathology-related tasks.

papers.title: Privacy Risks and Leakage Pathways in Agentic and Multi-Agent AI Systems
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
papers.summary: Agentic and multi-agent AI systems are increasingly deployed as part of operational systems, introducing autonomous planning, delegation, persistent memory, tool use, and inter-agent coordination into data-driven decision making. These architectural properties challenge prevailing privacy assumptions because leakage may arise structurally from autonomy, coordination, persistence, and composition rather than only from isolated model outputs. This article provides a structured synthesis of privacy risks and leakage pathways for agentic and multi-agent AI systems. We introduce a unifying abstraction that combines decentralized decision making with trace-based information-flow semantics, enabling reasoning about autonomy, coordination, persistent state, observability, and adversarial trace projections. Using this abstraction, we organize recurring privacy risks into five leakage pathways: autonomy-induced overexposure, coordination-driven information propagation, memory and persistent-state leakage, emergent and compositional inference, and observability and audit leakage. We further analyze why established privacy-enhancing technologies provide incomplete coverage in agentic settings, where static computation boundaries, single-agent assumptions, ephemeral state, and non-emergent behavior often fail. To ground the analysis, we implement a controlled multi-agent privacy sandbox with privacy-aware agents, tool-mediated workflows, adversarial trace projections, and LLM-backed validation. The results show that policy-checked privacy-aware execution reduces direct disclosure and adversarial inference advantage, while residual tool-mediated and semantic-hint leakage remains. The article concludes by proposing new privacy requirements for agentic and multi-agent AI systems.

                     To develop, as a proof-of-concept analysis, a machine learning model predicting early radiological treatment response in an elderly, single-center esophageal cancer (EC) cohort, and to test whether adding clinical factors to CT radiomics improves prediction. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     We retrospectively reviewed 189 patients with EC treated with definitive radiotherapy. Radiomic features were extracted from baseline contrast-enhanced CT. Following TRIPOD recommendations, a LASSO-penalized logistic regression (LASSO-LR) on the radiomic feature set was pre-specified as the primary model, with the number of predictors capped at five (events per variable [EPV] ≥ 10; 50 events).                        n

                       P

papers.title: From Information Security Governance to Data Protection Effectiveness: The Serial Mediating Roles of Security Policy Compliance and Cybersecurity Capability
papers.venue: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS)
papers.summary:
Purpose - This study examines the relationship between Information Security Governance (ISG) and Data Protection Effectiveness (DPE), focusing on the serial mediating roles of Security Policy Compliance (SPC) and Cybersecurity Capability (CC).
Design/methods/approach – A quantitative explanatory approach was employed using a cross-sectional survey of 300 respondents selected through purposive sampling in Indonesia. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire comprising 33 indicators across four constructs and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4.
Findings – The results revealed significant positive relationships between ISG and SPC (β = 0.493, p < 0.001), SPC and CC (β = 0.433, p < 0.001), and CC and DPE (β = 0.404, p < 0.001). The serial indirect relationship between ISG and DPE through SPC and CC was also significant (β = 0.086, p < 0.001). The model explained 45.4% of the variance in DPE.
Research implications/limitations – The findings suggest that effective data protection requires coordinated governance, consistent security policy compliance, and organizational cybersecurity capabilities. However, the cross-sectional design, purposive sampling, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal interpretation and generalizability.
Originality/value – This study integrates the Information Security Governance and Dynamic Capability perspectives within a Governance–Behavior–Capability–Outcome Framework. It extends existing cybersecurity research by identifying behavioral compliance and organizational capability as sequential mechanisms linking security governance with data protection effectiveness.

papers.title: Vulnerabilities and Defenses in Audio-Visual Attacks: A Survey From Audio to Multimodal Models
papers.summary: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and the cost of large amounts of data and resources, researchers are more inclined to use public datasets and fine-tune open-source MLLMs to achieve excellent performance in audiovisual related tasks. While this trend accelerates progress, it also introduces security risks. Empirical studies demonstrate that the latest MLLMs can be manipulated to generate harmful content through crafted inputs, including adversarial perturbations and malicious queries, bypassing internal safeguards. To gain a deeper comprehension of the inherent security vulnerabilities associated with audio-visual-based multimodal models, a series of surveys investigates various types of attacks, including adversarial and backdoor attacks. While existing surveys on audio-visual attacks provide a comprehensive overview, they are limited to specific types of attacks, which lack a unified review of various types of attacks. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a comprehensive and systematic review of audio-visual attacks, which include adversarial, backdoor, and jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we also review various types of attacks in the latest audio-visual-based MLLMs, a dimension notably absent in existing surveys. Drawing from extensive literature, this paper delineates both challenges and emergent trends for future research on audio-visual attacks and defenses.

papers.summary:
Complementary-label learning 
                     (CLL) is a weakly supervised learning paradigm designed for multiclass classification tasks. In CLL, algorithms are provided with complementary labels, which indicate the classes an instance does not belong to, rather than specifying its true class. With the growing research interest in CLL and the unique challenges it presents, particularly in handling incomplete and indirect supervision, a comprehensive and systematic overview of existing methodologies, results, and research directions has become increasingly essential. In this survey, we provide the first systematic synthesis of recent advances in CLL and offer three major contributions. First, we establish a structured taxonomy that clarifies foundational concepts, distinctive algorithmic strategies, key contributions, and their inherent limitations. Second, to support reproducibility and accelerate future research, we introduce a publicly available
                     open-source CLL toolkit 
                    that unifies key algorithm implementations and offers ready-to-use benchmarking pipelines. Third, we conduct an
                     extensive benchmarking 
                    study covering a wide spectrum of CLL algorithms, using standardized evaluation protocols across both synthetic, human-annotated, and VLM-annotated complementary-label datasets. This provides the most complete performance comparison currently available. Finally, we discuss current open research challenges and identify promising avenues for future investigation, emphasizing improvements to the practical applicability and robustness of CLL in real-world scenarios. Overall, this survey provides an up-to-date, in-depth resource on the evolving CLL landscape.

papers.venue: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research
papers.summary:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, is frequently complicated by persistent inflammation and sleep disturbance, both of which negatively affect disease control and quality of life. Melatonin, a key regulator of circadian rhythm, also exhibits anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory properties. Although several clinical trials have evaluated melatonin as an adjunctive therapy in IBD, its overall efficacy remains unclear. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials assessing exogenous melatonin supplementation in patients with IBD. Electronic databases (PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus) were searched until October 7, 2025. Primary outcomes included changes in disease activity indices and clinical remission. Secondary outcomes included inflammatory biomarkers, patient-reported outcomes, and safety. Random-effects models were used to pool effect estimates. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Five studies involving a total of 214 patients met the inclusion criteria. Melatonin supplementation was associated with a significant reduction in disease activity compared with standard therapy alone (standardized mean difference −0.96, 95% CI −1.60 to −0.32), although heterogeneity was substantial. Individual trials consistently reported earlier remission, improved maintenance of remission, or greater reductions in clinical activity indices with melatonin. Effects on systemic inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were variable and not consistently significant, while fecal calprotectin improved in one study. Improvements in sleep quality and selected quality-of-life domains were observed. Melatonin was generally well tolerated, with only mild and infrequent adverse events reported. 
                   
                   
                     Conclusions 
                     Current evidence suggests that melatonin may be a safe and potentially effective adjunctive therapy for improving clinical disease activity and patient-centered outcomes in IBD. Larger, high-quality randomized trials are required to confirm these findings and define its role in routine clinical practice.

papers.title: AI readiness and digital pedagogical competence as enablers of innovations in environmental management within higher education institutions: evidence from Vietnam
papers.venue: International Conference on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems (CHES)
papers.summary:
Purpose 
                     This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and digital pedagogical competence (DPC) are associated with lecturers’ perceptions of digital environmental governance innovation (DEGI) and perceived environmental performance in higher education institutions (HEIs). Moving beyond isolated green technologies, the study adopts a governance-oriented perspective to explain how individual digital capabilities among academic staff are linked to perceived sustainability-related outcomes through digitally enabled environmental governance innovation. 
                   
                   
                     Design/methodology/approach 
                     The study uses a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 1,525 academic staff working in Vietnamese HEIs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was used to test the proposed capability–governance–perception framework and to examine both direct and indirect relationships among the constructs. 
                   
                   
                     Findings 
                     The findings indicate that AI readiness (artificial intelligence readiness) is positively associated with DPC and lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI. DPC is also positively associated with governance innovation. Most importantly, lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI are strongly associated with perceived environmental performance and indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AIR and perceived environmental outcomes within the specified model. 
                   
                   
                     Research limitations/implications 
                     This study is based on cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from a single national context, which limits causal inference and statistical generalisability. The findings should therefore be interpreted as perception-based associations rather than evidence of objectively measured institutional environmental improvement. Future research could adopt longitudinal, comparative, multi-source or objective-indicator designs. 
                   
                   
                     Practical implications 
                     The findings suggest that HEIs should move beyond technology adoption alone and invest in human digital capabilities, sustainability dashboards, environmental data reporting systems and governance structures. Strengthening AIR and DPC among academic staff may support digitally mediated governance innovations for environmental management. 
                   
                   
                     Social implications 
                     By highlighting governance innovation as a perception-based pathway linking digital capabilities to perceived environmental performance, this study offers insights for HEIs seeking to strengthen their sustainability responsibilities. Digitally enabled environmental governance may support broader sustainability transitions, provided it is embedded within accountable institutional practices. 
                   
                   
                     Originality/value 
                     This study offers empirical evidence linking individual digital capabilities to perceived environmental management outcomes in higher education through governance innovation. It extends sustainability and digital transformation research by positioning AIR and DPC as enablers of perceived digitally driven environmental governance, particularly within a Global South context.

papers.title: Systemic privacy risks of personal data exposure through conversational large language model agents
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
papers.summary:
Abstract 
                   Conversational Large Language Model (LLM) agents, deployed quickly, have exposed unprecedented opportunities for personal information, from health data to financial information, to biometric identifiers. This critical enlightenment review investigates general privacy dangers in each of five areas: data leakage and memorization, adversarial extraction and prompt injection, inference and re-identification, surveillance and profiling and regulatory governance breakdown. We trace privacy threats from static data breaches to dynamic ones that have become part of an architecture, associated with neural memorization and contextual inference (2020–2026), using expert selection of primary studies and technical benchmark sources. Upon close examination, technical mitigations (differential privacy, federated learning and machine unlearning) prove successful to some extent when operating in controlled environments, but fail to provide complete protection in conversational environments. We combine classical theory on Privacy-Preserving Data Publishing (PPDP) with emerging threats from LLMs, and present a conflict-of-evidence analysis which reveals that privacy protections are particularly effective in structured environments with low risks, or with consumers actively responsible for maintaining them, but fail to adequately protect privacy in high-stakes domains without human control, technical safeguards, and legal liability. We systematically examine and analyze a dimension that has not been studied sufficiently: risks of data deletion and editing illusion, and introduce techniques for unlearning machines that leave behind traces that can be exploited by adversarial reconstruction. We support the multi-layered mitigation framework of PPDP principles, technical safeguards, and governance reform.

papers.summary:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     This study developed and validated a machine-learning model using biparametric MRI (bpMRI) that integrates clinical variables, Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) scores, and radiomics features to distinguish clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     This retrospective study included 458 patients with clinical and bpMRI data. Clinical predictors were identified via univariate and multivariate stepwise regression. Regions of interest (ROIs) were delineated on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps using 3D Slicer, and radiomics features were extracted with PyRadiomics. Optimal features were selected via dimensionality reduction and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Patients were split 7:3 into training and validation sets. LR, SVM, RF, and XGBoost were evaluated as candidate algorithms for the radiomics and combined models. The final algorithm was selected based on discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Model performance was assessed by discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]), calibration (calibration slope and intercept), and clinical utility (decision curve analysis within the 10%–60% threshold range). The selected model was then used to build a nomogram. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     
                      In the validation cohort, the clinical model, Radiomics LR, and Combined LR achieved AUCs of 0.843, 0.888, and 0.900, respectively. Combined LR significantly outperformed both the clinical model (
                       p 
                       < 0.001) and Radiomics LR (
                       p 
                       = 0.032). Combined LR showed a sensitivity of 0.841 and a calibration slope of 0.950 (intercept = −0.759). After balancing discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, Combined LR was selected to build a nomogram, which demonstrated good calibration and net benefit within the 10%–60% threshold range.
                     
                   
                   
                     Conclusion 
                     This nomogram integrates bpMRI radiomics, clinical variables, and PI-RADS scores and outperforms conventional radiomics and clinical models. It provides a non-invasive tool for risk stratification before biopsy and helps to reduce unnecessary biopsies.

papers.title: Community Monitoring and Project Resilience under Funding Uncertainty in Community-Based Projects in Kajiado County, Kenya.
papers.venue: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research
papers.summary: Community-based projects are critical in advancing socio-economic development in marginalized regions of Kenya, contributing to improved access to water, healthcare, education and livelihood opportunities. In Kajiado County, which hosts about 255 community-based projects and 53 youth groups supported by government agencies, NGOs and international development partners, nearly 40–45% of projects experience delays or interruptions owing to funding inconsistencies and up to 65% struggle after donor withdrawal. Community monitoring has emerged as a key mechanism for enhancing accountability, transparency and resilience, yet its influence on project sustainability under financial instability remains inadequately understood. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to examine the effect of community monitoring on project resilience under funding uncertainty in community-based projects in Kajiado County, Kenya. It specifically assessed the influence of frequency of tracking, citizen feedback mechanisms, data literacy levels and inclusivity of monitoring committees on project resilience. The study was anchored on the Participatory Development Theory, Stakeholder Theory, Adaptive Management Theory and Human Capital Theory. A descriptive and explanatory research design was adopted, targeting 32 major donor-funded community-based projects and 648 stakeholders comprising project committee members, beneficiaries, NGO representatives, local administrators and youth group leaders. A sample of 87 respondents was determined using Nassiuma's formula and selected through stratified random sampling. Primary data were collected using a structured questionnaire, and both descriptive and inferential statistical methods, namely Pearson correlation and multiple regression analysis, were used to analyse the data, which were presented in tables and discussed. The findings revealed that the four dimensions of community monitoring jointly explained 45.6% of the variation in project resilience. Citizen feedback mechanisms had the strongest positive and significant effect on project resilience, followed by data literacy levels and frequency of tracking, while inclusivity of monitoring committees had a positive and significant but comparatively weaker effect. The study, therefore, recommends that community-based projects should standardize monitoring and reporting schedules, ensure timely processing of community feedback, build stakeholders' capacity in data analysis and digital monitoring tools, and promote meaningful participation of marginalized groups in monitoring committees so as to strengthen project resilience under funding uncertainty in Kajiado County.

papers.title: 3D Convolutional Autoencoder with Spectral–Spatial Attention (3DCAE-SSA) for Anomaly Detection in Hyperspectral Imagery
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
papers.summary: Hyperspectral anomaly detection (HAD) refers to the process of identifying pixels or regions that are significantly different from the surrounding background signature of a hyperspectral image (HSI). HAD is highly challenging due to high spectral dimensionality, complex spatial patterns, subtle nature of the real-world environment, and limited knowledge about the signature of interest. This study develops a HAD algorithm combining three-Dimensional (3D) Convolutional Autoencoder (3DCAE), Spectral-Spatial Attention (SSA) and a robust hybrid loss. We use 3DCAE that employs 3D convolution layers (3DCLs) instead of fully connected layers to create a compact latent space from the input image, while the decoder uses deconvolution layers to recover the input image. We attach multi-headed spectral attention and multi-scale spatial attention that help to expand local receptive fields to global context and allow each voxel to attend to the other long-range voxels. In the proposed 3DCAE-SSA, to minimize the image reconstruction error, we introduce a hybrid robust loss to quantify the reconstruction error instead of using mean squared error (MSE) which is sensitive to outliers. To see the performance of the new algorithm, we build an error map based on a robust statistical Mahalanobis distance. For open access, Urban-4 dataset the AUC values show that the new algorithm performs significantly better having AUC value 99.76% than two existing algorithms: Auto-AD (97.47%), and GAED (99.24%).

papers.title: Bridging radiomics and histopathology: cross-modality consistency of radiomic features from CT to micro-CT in NSCLC
papers.summary:
Abstract 
                   
                     Objective 
                     
                      Radiomics extracts quantitative features from medical images that may provide non-invasive biomarkers of tumor biology and heterogeneity. However, few studies have explored radiomics on micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) or its transferability to clinical CT. This study investigates the reproducibility and the potential biological correlation of radiomic features across
                       in vivo 
                      CT,
                       ex vivo 
                      CT, and
                       ex vivo 
                      micro-CT in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
                     
                   
                   
                     Materials and methods 
                     
                      A retrospective cohort of 60 NSCLC patients with preoperative CT scans and surgical specimens was analyzed.
                       Ex vivo 
                      CT and micro-CT images were acquired and compared with
                       in vivo 
                      CT using standardized preprocessing, including normalization, resampling, and registration. Tumor regions of interest (ROIs) were semi-automatically segmented, and 93 radiomic features were extracted with Pyradiomics. Cross-modality reproducibility and associations with histotype were evaluated using Spearman correlation, intraclass correlation coefficient, Bland–Altman analysis, and Mann–Whitney
                       U 
                      test.
                     
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Normalization and volume matching improved feature repeatability, with the highest agreement observed in normalized datasets using subsampled ROIs. Four texture-based features consistently showed high reproducibility and potential biological correlation, likely reflecting intratumoral heterogeneity and variation in cell density: DependenceNonUniformity, GrayLevelNonUniformity (GLDM and GLRLM), and Coarseness (NGTDM). These features reliably distinguished adenocarcinoma from squamous cell carcinoma across modalities, confirming their stability and potential as candidate features for transferable biomarkers. 
                   
                   
                     Conclusion 
                     Harmonization and volume standardization are essential for cross-modality radiomic analyses. Stable texture features provide a potential transferable signature bridging micro-CT and clinical CT imaging in NSCLC, supporting their role as candidate features for further investigation in biologically oriented studies. 
                   
                   
                     Key Points 
                     
                       
                         Question 
                       
                      Micro-CT serves as an intermediate imaging scale enabling radiomic feature extraction from
                       ex vivo 
                      NSCLC tumors, allowing direct comparison with
                       in vivo 
                      and
                       ex vivo 
                      CT.
                     
                     
                       
                         Findings 
                       
                      Intensity normalization and volume-matched subsampling between
                       in vivo 
                      CT,
                       ex vivo 
                      CT, and micro-CT reduced cross-modality feature variability, improving feature reproducibility.
                     
                     
                       
                         Relevance statement 
                       
                      Normalization, volume matching, and cross-modality analysis support the identification of candidate texture features with consistent cross-scale behavior and exploratory associations with NSCLC histotype.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in National Security: Applications, Risks, and Governance Pathways
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
papers.summary: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), its applications have gradually expanded from the commercial and civilian sectors to national security fields such as military security, cybersecurity, and critical infrastructure protection. Using a literature review and case analysis approach, this article examines the main applications of AI in different security scenarios and the risks they bring. The study finds that AI can improve the information processing and response capabilities of the national security system by enhancing the efficiency of multi-source information processing, strengthening threat identification and prediction capabilities, and increasing the autonomy of military systems. However, enhanced AI capabilities do not necessarily lead to higher levels of security. Its national security applications face three interconnected risks: technical unreliability, malicious use, and strategic instability arising from the security dilemma. Therefore, this article argues that AI governance cannot rely solely on technological improvements. Instead, it requires a governance path comprised of technical safeguards, risk-based regulation, and international cooperation. This should be achieved through testing, auditing, human-in-the-loop mechanisms, and confidence-building measures (CBMs) to mitigate the risks posed by technological errors, malicious misuse, and strategic miscalculations. Overall, the key to AI governance is not restricting AI's entry into the national security domain, but rather establishing corresponding control, oversight, and international coordination mechanisms while enhancing its security capabilities.
